stimulus.text:
Saint-Domingue (the French colony on the western part of Hispaniola), about 1791:

| Group | Number |
|---|---|
| Enslaved Africans | about 500,000 |
| Free whites | about 30,000 |
| Free people of mixed race (gens de couleur) | about 30,000 |

Free people of mixed race owned about a third of the enslaved people on the island but were barred from political participation.
stimulus.source_note: Figures as given in Barron's AP U.S. History Premium, 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.6.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, C. The Impact of the American Revolution Abroad

stem: According to the table, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue outnumbered free people by about

options.misconception: The table's numbers are far more lopsided than two to one; 500,000 enslaved people face only 60,000 free people.
Four to one would mean 240,000 free people; the table counts only about 60,000 free people in all.
Six to one would mean about 83,000 free people; the table counts about 60,000, so the gap is wider still.

rationales.D: About 500,000 enslaved people faced about 60,000 free people — whites and free people of mixed race together — a ratio of roughly eight to one.
rationales.A: Two to one is far too small; the enslaved outnumbered the free by hundreds of thousands.
rationales.B: Four to one understates the gap; 500,000 against 60,000 is more than eight to one.
rationales.C: Six to one still understates it; the table's numbers give roughly eight enslaved people for every free person.
rationales.general:
1. Add the free. About 30,000 whites plus about 30,000 free people of mixed race: 60,000 in all.
2. Compare. About 500,000 enslaved people against 60,000 free people.
3. Divide. 500,000 divided by 60,000 is a little over eight — about eight to one.
Remember: a ratio needs both sides added up first — total the free before you divide.
